original_value: A series of recent studies formulated the diffusion prediction problem as a sequence prediction task and proposed several sequential models based on recurrent neural networks. However, non-sequential properties exist in real diffusion cascades, which do not strictly follow the sequential assumptions of previous work. In this paper, we propose a hierarchical diffusion attention network (HiDAN), which adopts a non-sequential framework and two-level attention mechanisms, for diffusion prediction. At the user level, a dependency attention mechanism is proposed to dynamically capture historical user-to-user dependencies and extract the dependency-aware user information. At the cascade (i.e., sequence) level, a time-aware influence attention is designed to infer possible future user's dependencies on historical users by considering both inherent user importance and time decay effects. Significantly higher effectiveness and efficiency of HiDAN over state-of-the-art sequential models are demonstrated when evaluated on three real diffusion datasets. The further case studies illustrate that HiDAN can accurately capture diffusion dependencies.

result.paraphrase: Recent studies have framed diffusion prediction as a sequence prediction problem and introduced several recurrent neural network–based sequential models. Yet real diffusion cascades also exhibit non-sequential characteristics, so they do not fully adhere to the sequential assumptions made in earlier work. To address this, we present a hierarchical diffusion attention network (HiDAN) for diffusion prediction, using a non-sequential framework with two levels of attention. At the user level, a dependency attention mechanism dynamically captures historical user-to-user dependencies and derives dependency-aware user representations. At the cascade, or sequence, level, a time-aware influence attention mechanism is used to estimate a future user’s possible dependencies on past users by accounting for both intrinsic user importance and time-decay effects. Evaluations on three real diffusion datasets show that HiDAN is markedly more effective and efficient than state-of-the-art sequential models, and case studies further show that it can accurately model diffusion dependencies.
